```{r, include = FALSE}
if (requireNamespace("pkgload", quietly = TRUE)) {
  pkgload::load_all(export_all = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
}
options(mcp_quiet = TRUE)
bayesplot::bayesplot_theme_set(bayesplot::theme_default(base_size = 11, base_family = "sans"))
set.seed(42)
```

`mcp` supports group-level effects (also called random effects) in both the predictor and change-point parts of a formula. The syntax follows `lme4` and `brms`: `(1|group)` specifies a group-level intercept, `(factor||group)` specifies independent group coefficients, `fixef()` reports population-level coefficients, `ranef()` reports group-level deviations, and `coef()` reports their sums, i.e., the group-specific coefficients and change points.

This article in brief:

 * Predictor and change-point group-level effects
 * How group-level effects apply across segments
 * How to simulate group-level change-point deviations
 * Get posteriors using `ranef(fit)` for deviations or `coef(fit)` for group-specific values
 * Plot using `plot(fit, facet_by="my_group")` and `plot_pars(fit, pars = "group", type = "dens_overlay", ncol = 3)` ([more on plotting](../articles/plotting.html)).
 * How group-specific change points are restricted to the observed range and ordered.
 * The article on modeling standard deviation via `sigma()` contains [another group-level change-point example](../articles/dpar.html).

```{r}
library(mcp)
future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 3)
```


# Specifying group-level change points

You specify group-level effects using the familiar [`lmer`](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/lme4/versions/1.1-21/topics/lmer) and `brms` syntax `(1|group)`. Inside `cp()`, this models a group-specific deviation from the population-level change point. For example:

```{r}
model = list(
  y ~ 1,                  # Intercept_1
    ~ cp((1|id)) + 0 + x  # cp_1, cp_1_id_sd, cp_1_id[i]
)
```

You can have multiple group-level change points, but they must use the same grouping factor so their group-specific change points can be ordered within each group:

```{r}
model = list(
  y ~ 1,                   # Intercept_1
    ~ cp((1|id)) + 0 + x,  # cp_1, cp_1_id_sd, cp_1_id[i]
    ~ cp((1|id)) + 0,      # cp_2, cp_2_id_sd, cp_2_id[i]
    ~ cp((1|id)) + 1       # cp_3, cp_3_id_sd, cp_3_id[i]
)
```

For change point $i$ and group $g$, the hierarchy is

$$
\kappa_{ig} \sim \operatorname{Normal}(cp_i, cp_{i,\mathrm{sd}}), \qquad
cp_{i,\mathrm{id}[g]} = \kappa_{ig} - cp_i,
$$

where $\kappa_{ig}$ is the group-specific location. Thus `cp_i_id[g]` is the reported deviation and `cp_i_id_sd` is the SD of the normal distribution *before truncation* (see below). The deviations are not forced to sum to zero.

The hierarchy is subject to $x_{\min} < \kappa_{1g} < \cdots < \kappa_{Kg} < x_{\max}$. Thus, if adjacent change points both vary, their group-specific locations are ordered against each other—not against the adjacent population-level change point. Internally, JAGS samples $\kappa_{ig}$ directly for efficiency.

Because of this truncation, the realized SD of the group-specific change points is smaller than `cp_i_id_sd`, and their mean is pulled away from $cp_i$ when $cp_i$ is near a boundary. When `cp_i_id_sd` is large relative to the distance between these bounds, the truncated normal approaches a uniform distribution, so the data carry little information about how large `cp_i_id_sd` is. Its posterior then has a long upper tail that mostly reflects the prior.

Unlike predictor group-level effects, a change-point group-level effect applies only at the change point where it is included.

# Predictor group-level effects

The same syntax in the predictor part gives each group a deviation from the population-level intercept:

```{r}
model = list(
  y ~ 1 + (1|id),  # Starts group-level intercept
  ~ 0 + x,         # (1|id) not included, so group intercepts end at cp_1
  ~ 1 + (0|id),    # (0|id) turns it off
  ~0 + same((1|id), as = 1)  # Reuse group-level intercept from segment 1
)
```

Group-level terms follow the [rules for how segments connect](../articles/formulas.html#how-segments-connect), separately for each grouping factor and distributional parameter. Group intercepts apply only in segments that include them, so each group can jump at a joined change point; use `same((1|id))` to keep them. Group slopes on `x`, such as `(0 + x||id)`, are x-terms: they join until a disjoined segment (`~ 1 + ...`), a later group intercept for the same grouping factor, or `(0|id)`, which ends all group terms for `id`.

Notice `same()` above. It reuses the complete group-level term from the source segment (deviations and SD), never a subset of it. Reused group slopes are still measured from the current change point. The same syntax works inside `sigma()` and other distributional parameters. See `mcp_example("group_mu")`.


Use `||` for independent group-level slopes and factor coefficients:

```{r}
model = list(
  y ~ 1 + state + (state||id),
  ~ 0 + x
)
```

With the default treatment coding, `(state||id)` contains a group-level intercept and one group-level deviation for each non-reference contrast of `state`. `(0 + state||id)` instead gives each factor level its own group-level coefficient. Similarly, `(1 + z||id)` specifies independent group-level intercepts and slopes on a numeric predictor `z`. Each coefficient has its own population-level SD.

The population-level and group-level formulas need not contain the same coefficients. For example, `y ~ 1 + (0 + state||id)` has a population-level intercept but only group-specific state coefficients.

Group-level intercepts also work inside distributional formulas:

```{r}
model = list(
  y ~ 1 + (1|id) + sigma(1 + (1|id))
)
```

This model has group-level deviations in both the conditional mean and log-SD. The `||` syntax works inside distributional formulas too, for example `sigma(1 + (state||id))`.

A later group intercept starts the group terms afresh. Thus, if `(state||id)` is followed in a later segment by `(1||id)`, only the new intercept deviations apply from that segment onward. In a joined segment, a group-level term without an intercept, such as `(0 + x||id)`, joins earlier group slopes, while `(0|id)` ends all group terms for `id`.

Multi-coefficient terms with `|`, such as `(1 + x|id)`, would imply correlated group coefficients and are not yet supported; use `(1 + x||id)` for independent coefficients. Group-level terms inside `ar()` and `ma()` are also not supported.

Like change-point deviations, predictor deviations are not constrained to sum to zero. They have an ordinary mean-zero hierarchical normal distribution, matching multilevel regression in `lme4` and `brms`. For example, `(1|id)` in segment 1 creates the deviation vector `Intercept_1_id` and its population-level SD parameter `Intercept_1_id_sd`. `(state||id)` additionally creates names such as `stateB_1_id` and `stateB_1_id_sd`; inside `sigma()`, the corresponding names start with `sigma`.



# Simulating group-level change points
Let us simulate group-specific deviations in the change point between a plateau and a slope:

```{r}
model = list(
  y ~ 1,                  # Intercept_1
    ~ cp((1|id)) + 0 + x  # cp_1, cp_1_id_sd, cp_1_id[i]
)
```

This follows the same interface as predictor group-level effects: supply the population-level SD and `fit$simulate()` draws one deviation per group from the same truncated normal hierarchy as the JAGS model (see above), keeping each group-specific change point within its bounds. The deviations are therefore not centered exactly on zero.

```{r}
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)
group_levels = c("Clark", "Louis", "Batman", "Batgirl", "Spiderman", "Jane")
df = data.frame(
  x = runif(length(group_levels) * 30, 0, 100),  # 30 data points for each
  id = rep(group_levels, each = 30),  # the group names
  y = 1
)
empty = mcp(model, data = df, sample = FALSE)

df$y = empty$simulate(empty, df,
  # Population-level:
  Intercept_1 = 20, x_2 = 0.5, cp_1 = 50, sigma_1 = 2,
  
  # Draw group-level deviations with this SD
  cp_1_id_sd = 15)

head(df)
```

For models with multiple group-level change points, `fit$simulate()` draws the deviations in change-point order, truncated so each group-specific change point lies after its preceding one, just like the JAGS model. The result:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(df, aes(x=x, y=y)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~id)
```


# Summarise and plot group-level effects
Fitting the model is simple:

```{r}
fit = mcp(model, data = df)
```

If we just use `plot(fit)`, we would see all points in one plot. We want to facet by `id`, so:

```{r}
plot(fit, facet_by = "id")
```

It seems that `mcp` recovered the group-specific change points well. There is a lot of information in these data because the population-level intercept and slopes on either side of the change point are common to all participants (`id`).

`summary(fit)` returns posterior summaries for the population-level parameters, and `fixef(fit)` for the population-level coefficients. To get the group-level deviations (random effects), use:

```{r, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
mcp::ranef(fit)
```

Inspecting the `sim` and `match` columns, we see that the simulated deviations lie within the intervals. However, the intervals are wide because the deviations trade off against the population-level `cp_1`, which is informed by only six groups. In this case, the simulated deviations happen to be mostly positive, so the model attributes their shared shift to `cp_1`, and all estimated deviations sit below their simulated values by a similar amount.

The group-specific change points (`cp_1 + cp_1_id[g]`) are much more precise, as seen in the plot above. Get them using `coef(fit)`, which adds the population-level parameter to each deviation, as in `lme4` and `brms`:

```{r, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
coef(fit)
```

Because the deviations are relative to `cp_1`, they share its estimation error. If `cp_1` misses its simulated value, the deviations tend to miss with it, even when every group's change point is recovered. The `match` column of `coef(fit)` checks the group-specific change points directly.

Prediction methods include all group-level effects by default. Set `group_effects = FALSE` (or `NA`, as in `brms`) for population-level predictions, `group_effects = "cp"` for the group-level effects in the change-point part, `group_effects = "predictor"` for those in the predictor part, or supply parameter names such as `group_effects = "cp_1_id"`. Use `*` as a wildcard, e.g., `"cp_*"` or `"*_id"`. `ranef(fit)` deliberately remains simple and returns all group-level deviations.

Good convergence is not always as obvious as in this example. While `plot_pars(fit)` shows population-level parameters only, you can select the group-level deviations with `"group"`:

```{r}
plot_pars(fit, pars = "group", type = "trace", ncol = 3, npars = NULL)
```

The `ncol` argument controls the number of columns. Group-level effects often have many levels, so this is useful for viewing all deviations.

Using `pars = "group"` plots all group-level deviations. To select one group-level effect, use a regular expression in `regex_pars`; for example, `^` anchors the start of a parameter name:

```{r}
plot_pars(fit, regex_pars = "^cp_1_id", type = "dens_overlay", ncol = 2, npars = NULL)
```

You can also do posterior predictive checks with facets. For a single-response model like this, it adds little over `plot(fit, facet_by = "id")`, but it is a standard check that many will be familiar with:

```{r}
pp_check(fit, facet_by = "id")
```




# Priors for group-level effects

*[Brief overview of all default priors](../articles/default_priors.html#summary-reference-table)*

You can see the priors of the model like this:

```{r, R.options = list(width = 9999)}
prior_summary(fit)
```

`cp_1_id_sd` is the SD of the normal distribution, before truncation, governing the `cp_1_id` deviations. Unlike predictor group-level effects, change-point locations are also bounded by the observed range of $x$ and ordered within each group.

For predictor group-level effects (e.g., `(state || id)`), the SDs default to the `brms` half-Student-t prior on the response scale, `dt(0, max(2.5, mad(y)), 3) T(0, )`, with slope SDs divided by `sd(column)`. Log, logit, and probit links and distributional parameters use other scales; see [default priors on group-level effects](../articles/default_priors.html#default-priors-on-group-level-effects).

Here is the JAGS code for the model used in this article:
